metadata.title: Approval Rating Self-Correction (Balancing Example)
metadata.description: A simple 3-node balancing loop used in the appendix to teach how to read a causal loop diagram. High approval emboldens a president to take political risks, which produces voter backlash, which pulls approval back down toward equilibrium.
metadata.author: US Government Intelligent Textbook

nodes.label: Approval Rating
nodes.description: The percentage of Americans who say they approve of the president's job performance.

nodes.label: Risky Policy Choices
nodes.description: Politically controversial moves — unpopular vetoes, contested executive orders, ambitious legislation — that a president feels free to attempt when their political capital is high.

nodes.label: Voter Backlash
nodes.description: Public anger, protest, and negative media coverage that follows a controversial decision.

edges.description: A president with high approval has political capital to spend, so they attempt more controversial moves.
Controversial decisions provoke opposition, protest, and negative media coverage.
Public anger drives the president's approval rating back down. This single negative edge is what makes the loop balancing.

loops.label: B1: Approval Self-Correction
loops.description: A built-in stabilizer of American politics: every president eventually overreaches when their approval is high, and the public pulls them back.
loops.behavior_pattern: Oscillation around a slowly-falling average — most presidents end their term less popular than they started.
